story: King Sagara, great-grandfather of Bhagiratha, once performed a great horse sacrifice, but the sacrificial horse was stolen by the god Indra and hidden in the underworld realm of Patala, where the sage Kapila was meditating. Sagara's 60,000 sons found the horse there and disturbed Kapila with their noise; enraged, the sage reduced them all to ashes with his fiery gaze. The duty of performing their funeral rites passed down through generations until it fell to Bhagiratha. After becoming king, he went to the Himalayas to practice austerities and invoke the goddess Ganga, asking her to descend from heaven to earth. She warned that her fall would be too powerful to bear unless the god Shiva agreed to catch her in his hair. Bhagiratha then performed a thousand-year penance to Shiva, who agreed and let Ganga flow through his matted locks for a thousand years before releasing a single drop, which became the river on earth. The river flowed to Patala and performed the funeral rites for Sagara's sons. Along the way, the river flooded the hermitage of the sage Jahnu, who swallowed it in anger; only after Bhagiratha's pleading did Jahnu release the river through his ear. Bhagiratha then ruled again, his people prospering. He was known for gifting many cows to a sage, and he married his daughter to another sage before dying. Separately, it is said his father Dilipa died childless, so two of Dilipa's widows conceived Bhagiratha together, though the child was born deformed until a crippled sage transformed him into a strong youth.
